item.title: Causal adaptive intensity estimation for non-stationary point processes: a Kalman-kernel duality framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.24018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating the instantaneous conditional intensity of a non-stationary point process from a single realization of discrete event timestamps is a fundamental problem in computational neuroscience, quantitative finance, and network monitoring. Traditional adaptive kernel methods achieve variable bandwidths through Abramson's square-root law, yet existing implementations require non-causal access to the complete event record and incur $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ or at best $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ computational cost. Causal alternatives based on reciprocal inter-arrival times, meanwhile, suffer from systematic divergence under Poisson and bursty arrival dynamics due to Jensen's inequality. This paper addresses both limitations by establishing a formal duality between steady-state Kalman filtering and adaptive exponential kernel smoothing. An endogenous state-space observer is constructed in which Poisson counting statistics dictate the measurement noise ($R \propto \lambda$) and geometric diffusion governs the process volatility ($Q \propto \lambda^2$). Under these physically motivated axioms, the algebraic Riccati equation autonomously yields an effective smoothing bandwidth scaling as $\tau \propto \lambda^{-1/2}$, giving a causal, recursive, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per-step realization of square-root adaptive bandwidth scaling. A second-order constant-velocity extension produces a $\lambda^{-1/4}$ scaling that reduces approximation bias, and a probabilistic dormant-state gating mechanism suppresses phantom intensity leakage during structural zeros. Synthetic benchmarks together with neural and financial data show that the observer adapts across orders of magnitude in intensity with an empirical per-step cost of approximately 30\,$\mu$s.
item.dc:creator: Hanwu Qin, Dianhai Wang, Meng Zhang, Huangjun You, Zhengyi Cai

item.title: Extrinsic MANOVA for Oriented Projective Shapes
item.description: arXiv:2610.24021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For configurations of landmarks reconstructed from camera images, classical projective shape analysis identifies antipodal spherical representatives of projective coordinates, while oriented projective shape (OPS) retains their distinction. In 3D, a fixed oriented-projective coordinate representation of a OPS is point on product of 3D spheres. We develop nonparametric multisample inference for equality of population extrinsic means on this product. Quaternion multiplication helps create a global orthonormal tangent frame field, in which we obtain explicit extrinsic covariance blocks that preserve dependence between registered landmarks. A covariance-weighted MANOVA statistic has a chi-square null limit under nonfocality of distributions and positive-definite extrinsic covariance assumptions. An inverse-free discrepancy has a weighted chi-square limit when covariance matrices may be singular, and centered, groupwise nonparametric bootstrap procedures are justified asymptotically. We apply a fixed-observed-covariance nonparametric bootstrap version of the weighted statistic to 31 seven-landmark facial reconstructions from five subjects. Separate tests at the right inner brow and chin reject equality of the five OPS mean directions after Bonferroni adjustment. The analysis concerns a common mixed-sign frame domain and marginal landmarks; it does not establish pairwise subject differences or a joint six-dimensional facial test.
item.dc:creator: Musab Alamoudi, Robert L. Paige, Victor Patrangenaru

item.title: Geometry-Adaptive Clustering on High-Dimensional Tori
item.description: arXiv:2610.24079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multivariate angular data lie on a torus, but clustering methods often use the flat torus. We introduce curved-torus energy (CTE), a position-dependent dissimilarity based on restricted Riemannian path energy and minimization over winding classes. CTE has a certified finite winding reduction, an exact flat endpoint, a geodesic upper bound, and stability with respect to the geometry parameter. For label-free geometry selection, we propose CEHS-HM, a held-out criterion for selecting the warping parameter at a specified clustering resolution. We establish a finite-grid population-score regret bound and also consider joint geometry-resolution selection over finite candidate grids. Controlled experiments on $\mathbb{T}^3$ show that CTE agrees with the flat method at zero warping and becomes more useful as geometric warping increases. Additional experiments show that the CEHS-selected geometry should be viewed as a data-adaptive clustering choice rather than as an estimator of a generative deformation parameter. Under a product-von-Mises mechanism, the selector tends toward the flat endpoint when curvature is unnecessary. On ILE protein torsion data, the proposed method identifies a stable five-mode representation of joint backbone-side-chain conformation.
item.dc:creator: Surojit Biswas, Soumyadip Paik, Buddhananda Banerjee

item.title: Kriging Beyond Gaussianity: Fixed-Domain Asymptotic Optimality
item.description: arXiv:2610.24115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under squared-error loss, the optimal predictor of a non-Gaussian random field is its conditional mean, which may be difficult to compute. We consider a broad class of non-Gaussian random fields obtained by transforming finitely many independent Gaussian fields sharing a common correlation function, and study when kriging entails no first-order loss in mean squared prediction error (MSPE) under fixed-domain asymptotics. We compare the observed-data conditional mean, kriging with the observed covariance, kriging with the latent correlation, and a latent-information oracle. These predictors satisfy a finite-sample MSPE ordering. Under conditions linking transformation regularity to the high-frequency decay of the latent spectral density, all four MSPEs are asymptotically equivalent. For radially nonincreasing spectral densities with polynomial tails, the required regularity order is independent of both the spatial dimension and the number of latent fields. Exponential correlation also yields finite-sample bounds. Examples include Weibull, skew-Gaussian, and copula-based fields, while numerical comparisons illustrate finite-sample differences. Counterexamples show why covariance structure and first-order transformation regularity alone are insufficient. Finally, standardized prediction errors converge to a Gaussian scale mixture, which is standard normal exactly when the transformation's gradient norm is almost surely constant.
item.dc:creator: Moreno Bevilacqua, Hector Araya

item.title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.24147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: lepidoptera is an open-source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. A pre-built mechanism library covers all nine combinations of continuous, categorical, and ordinal parent and child types, removing the need for users to implement type-specific sampling from scratch. A vine copula mechanism estimates the full joint dependence structure from observed data using pair-copula constructions and the Rosenblatt conditional-simulation algorithm, supporting over twenty copula families. Individual-level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population-level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre-fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. Three worked illustrations spanning clinical trial planning, emergency-ward capacity analysis, and epidemiological mediation analysis demonstrate the package's scope.
item.dc:creator: Danilo Augusto Sarti

item.title: Topological Learning under Sparsity through Huberized Distance Functionals
item.description: arXiv:2610.24170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning topological structure from sparsely contaminated data requires robust statistical methods, as even a small fraction of atypical observations can substantially distort the inferred topology. This article introduces a robust framework for topological learning through the Huberized Distance-to-Measure, which provides a robust filtration-generating functional for persistent homology. We establish large-sample properties of the proposed functional, and show that the associated filtration induces stable and consistent persistence diagrams. We further derive a maximum bias bound for persistence diagrams in bottleneck distance, thereby providing a quantitative measure of the sparseness associated with topological inference. The practical utility of the methodology thorough testing of statistical hypothesis problem is illustrated for a seven-circle packing configuration under sparse contamination, where it recovers the underlying topological structure. Its applicability to real data is further demonstrated through an analysis of the M-ferritin protein structure, where the method identifies a persistent $H_2$ feature corresponding to the iron-storage cavity.
item.dc:creator: Tuhin Subhra Mahato, Subhra Sankar Dhar

item.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.24178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. One objective is to determine which variables are associated with a covariate via the testing of multiple null hypotheses, say $H_m:\beta_m = 0$ for $m = 1, 2, ..., M$ where each $\beta_m$ is a regression parameter. The standard approach computes a $p$-value for each null hypothesis and applies some false discovery rate (FDR) method to determine which null hypotheses are rejected, i.e. which variables can be discovered as associated with the covariate. However, even if data are ``well modeled'', this approach tends to provide a misleading list of discoveries in that some ``uninteresting'' negligible associations ($\beta_m \approx 0$) are discovered, while other interesting associations are not. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:\beta_m\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Asare, Pratyaydipta Rudra, Joshua Habiger

item.title: Stochastic models with power-law trends: An analysis of Bitcoin price dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.24270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical studies have identified power-law scaling and long-memory dynamics in Bitcoin prices. To capture these features, we propose stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with a power-law trend (PLT) for modeling long-term price behavior. As a starting point, we introduce a PLT driven by a Wiener process, where the log-price follows a trend linear in log time. We explicitly derive the SDE solution, provide estimation procedures, and analyze its asymptotic properties. We extend the framework to more general driving noises. A Levy-driven PLT incorporates jump behavior, whereas fractional Brownian motion captures long-range dependence. The model is extended with a power-law volatility. We present a Monte Carlo simulation study that explores the estimator's applicability under jump-diffusion, Variance Gamma, alpha-stable, and fBm noise, and under daily, weekly, and monthly sampling. To highlight our framework's applicability, we model daily Bitcoin prices, compare the PLT model with geometric Brownian motion, and select the driving noise using out-of-sample Monte Carlo forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Alex Bomfim, Marta Calvache, Felipe Quintino

item.title: Higher Order Risk Comparisons of Oracle Calibrated Global Local Priors
item.description: arXiv:2610.24352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-order minimaxity offers limited guidance for choosing among global-local shrinkage priors, since different local-tail distributions can yield the same leading risk. Comparisons at a common global scale may also be misleading, as the scale interacts with the shape of the local prior. We study the worst-case squared-error risks of posterior means in sparse Gaussian normal-means estimation, allowing each prior its own risk-minimizing global scale. For local-variance priors with polynomial tails and logarithmic corrections, we characterize the calibrations that retain first- and second-order minimaxity and derive the asymptotic form of the unrestricted oracle scale. Even after this optimization, differences in risk remain. The polynomial tail index, logarithmic tail exponent and a scale-invariant higher-order correction distinguish priors at successively finer orders. In particular, the horseshoe has smaller asymptotic oracle risk than the horseshoe+, despite the latter's additional logarithmic tail factor. We also establish the calibration accuracy needed to preserve these differences and sufficient conditions for their stability under high-dimensional Gaussian regression designs.
item.dc:creator: Dongu Han

item.title: Adaptive Model-Switch Thermodynamic Integration: A Bayes Factor Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2610.24354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayes factors are a widely used model comparison criterion, but are often quite challenging and computationally expensive to estimate well. We propose a variation of the model-switch thermodynamic integration method for estimating Bayes factors that decreases the variance of the estimator and essentially eliminates integration error. We choose samples whose density in $\beta$ is proportional to the standard deviation of previously drawn samples. Rather than averaging many samples at each $\beta$, we use a very dense set of $\beta$ values, collecting one sample at each in order of increasing $\beta$ and one sample at each in order of decreasing $\beta$ to minimize "thermic lag". We study our procedure with a toy model (based loosely on some signal recovery problems). In this model we find that adaptive sampling gives us a 2.7-fold decrease in the spread of the estimated Bayes factor. We test our procedure both drawing directly from the posterior distribution and using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Malnati, Megan Kralj, Ken D. Olum

item.title: Nash Equilibrium Individualized Treatment Regimes under Network Interference
item.description: arXiv:2610.24357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network interference creates a fundamental tension in optimal individualized treatment regime learning: maximizing overall population outcomes may come at the expense of some individuals' outcomes. Existing optimal individualized treatment regime methods under interference primarily target population-level objectives without accounting for individual optimality. Motivated by this tension, we introduce Nash equilibrium individualized treatment regimes, or simply Nash regimes, which directly target individual optimality under interference. Under a Nash regime, no individual can improve their conditional expected outcome through unilateral deviation when all other individuals follow the regime. We establish conditions for the existence of Nash regimes. When no exact Nash regime exists, we introduce an $\alpha^*$-Nash regime as an alternative target that minimizes regret relative to individual optimality. We then develop Nash learning, a doubly robust procedure for estimating the proposed regimes. Under a super-population random-graph framework accommodating both sparse and dense networks, we characterize how network sparsity and treatment assignment mechanisms affect estimation performance. Simulations and a real-data application demonstrate that Nash learning improves individual optimality while maintaining competitive population-level performance.
item.dc:creator: Junwen Xia, Jingxiao Zhang, Dehan Kong

item.title: The Geometry of Informativeness: A Bregman-Centroid Diagnostic for Partial Pooling in Multisite Trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.24398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two multisite trials can have the same informativeness yet differ in how reliably individual site effects can be estimated. We show that the informativeness index averages site-specific reliabilities on the logit scale and is a Bregman centroid under Bernoulli-Kullback-Leibler divergence. This explains the geometric mean of sampling variances and yields a measure of profile dispersion. Under stated conditions, we relate profile dispersion to estimation error and show when balanced allocation maximizes informativeness at fixed total enrollment. Simulations show that estimator performance depends on the reliability profile and whether the target is individual effects, ranks, or their distribution. An online credit recovery trial illustrates the diagnostics and their conditional posterior uncertainty. We recommend reporting informativeness with arithmetic mean reliability and profile dispersion. The accompanying R package poolinfo provides tools for computing the diagnostics, posterior summaries, and design calculations.
item.dc:creator: JoonHo Lee

item.title: Correcting Bartlett factor-score error for latent covariates in partially linear double machine learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.24564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Substituting Bartlett factor scores for latent covariates leaves factor-score error that does not vanish as the sample grows and biases the adjusted structural coefficient. We propose Croon-DML, which subtracts the factor-score error covariance implied by the measurement model from the cross-fitted estimating equation of partially linear double/debiased machine learning (DML), and establish identification, Neyman orthogonality with respect to the conditional means, consistency, and asymptotic normality. Residual bias after correction comes from learning the conditional means of the factor scores: signal learning error, and noise fitting, in which the learner also fits the factor-score error. Signal learning error largely cancels when the three conditional means share a common penalty, and noise fitting by a linear smoother can be computed from its weights alone, so we also subtract it (Croon-DML-R). Across 12 Monte Carlo conditions, Croon-DML reduced the absolute bias of uncorrected DML by 66-95%, and the bias of Croon-DML-R with a common penalty differed from that of an oracle estimator using the true latent variables by at most 0.004. In an illustration with public longitudinal data, the correction was 15% of the latent-covariate adjustment; its size reflected the latent-covariate coefficients rather than the residualized reliabilities.
item.dc:creator: Eunjeong Song, Sehee Hong

item.title: The LR1 Lifetime Distribution: Properties, Nonmonotone Hazard, and Statistical Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.24575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The LR1 distribution links an exponential lifetime and a four-stage gamma lifetime through a single positive parameter $\lambda$. Their rates, $2\lambda$ and $\lambda/2$, have a fixed ratio, whereas the exponential mixing probability $\lambda^2/(1+\lambda^2)$ changes with the parameter. This restriction produces a hazard that decreases near zero and eventually increases toward $\lambda/2$ for every $\lambda>0$. We establish this behavior analytically and obtain an explicit parameter threshold separating decreasing densities from densities with an interior local peak. Distributional calculations provide survival probabilities, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order statistics, and reliability summaries. The density at zero establishes identifiability, and strict decrease of the mean ensures a unique moment estimate for every positive sample mean. Likelihood inference includes the score, observed information, a constrained expectation--maximization algorithm, and asymptotic confidence limits; spacing estimation and the likelihood under independent right censoring are also described. Eight Monte Carlo settings, comprising 4,000 generated datasets, quantify the error of likelihood and moment estimators and the coverage of log-scale intervals. The results apply in a fixed working time unit and concern mathematical properties and correctly specified simulation, rather than demonstrated superiority on observed data.
item.dc:creator: Lalita Singh

item.title: Score-optimized copula coupling for multivariate ensemble post-processing
item.description: arXiv:2610.24591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Univariate post-processing techniques can provide calibrated marginal predictive distributions, however, their application may distort or remove dependencies between forecast dimensions. This paper introduces Score-Optimized Copula Coupling (SOCC), a two-stage multivariate post-processing method that estimates a dependence template by minimizing a weighted combination of the energy score (ES) and variogram score (VS). An extended variant additionally incorporates calibration penalties based on average rank and band depth. We evaluate SOCC using 2-m temperature and wind-speed ensemble forecasts and compare it with well-established empirical and parametric copula-based multivariate post-processing methods. In both case studies, all considered SOCC variants significantly outperform the best-performing reference method in terms of ES and VS. The regularized Dawid-Sebastiani score provides further evidence of improved dependence modelling, particularly for the Combined SOCC variants for wind speed. Multivariate rank diagnostics nevertheless reveal trade-offs between improvements in these scores and different aspects of multivariate calibration.
item.dc:creator: M\'aria Lakatos

item.title: Nesting or resolution? Facility proxies for variance estimation versus confounding adjustment in claims data without facility identifiers
item.description: arXiv:2610.24679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In claims databases, facility identifiers are often removed during de-identification, leaving only coarse attributes such as bed size. Yet facility information is needed for variance estimation, confounding adjustment and assessment of treatment availability. We examined whether accreditation-gated billing items can build strata standing for hospitals, and how to construct a facility proxy for each use. In 1,730,736 adults undergoing surgery (Medical Data Vision database, Japan, 2019-2023), we built marker-pattern strata from 66 accreditation-gated receipt codes (markers) and evaluated each grouping against a true facility identifier in an insurer-based database (DeSC Healthcare) and in simulation. The variance explained by the marker-pattern strata decreased with the extent to which a variable was patient- rather than hospital-determined ($R^2$ 0.921 for an accreditation item, 0.036 for sex). For variance estimation, the supplied-attribute cells, which can merge but never split hospitals, kept the type I error rate at 4.8% with a wild cluster bootstrap, against 5.4% for the true identifier and 39% when clustering was ignored; every finer marker-based grouping did worse. For adjustment, evaluated with real facility-level confounders and simulated null exposures, the marker pattern removed 51% of the confounding related to accreditation-linked facility characteristics, against 8% for the cells. The proportion of patients in groups mixing hospitals with and without the relevant accreditation was 49% for the marker pattern against 98% for the cells. No single facility proxy serves every purpose: nesting governs variance estimation, and resolution governs adjustment and treatment availability. Without a facility identifier, the supplied-attribute cells can carry the standard errors, and marker-pattern strata are worth considering for the other two uses.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Nonomiya, Tomoka Matsuura, Ryota Kawai, Andreas Dengel, Koichi Kise, Wakaba Fukushima, Ayumi Shintani

item.title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes
item.description: arXiv:2610.24911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint-life insurance often involves several lifetimes subject to censoring at known dates. We construct prediction regions by reducing the lifetime vector to a suitable scalar outcome. We first characterise the reduction maps for which arbitrary componentwise censoring becomes ordinary right censoring. These maps are minima of coordinatewise nondecreasing transformations, with upper orthants as prediction regions. Under a common censoring date, the admissible class also includes the first-death and last-survivor times. Applying univariate weighted split-conformal calibration to the reduced outcomes then gives finite-sample marginal coverage with known retention probabilities under conditionally independent censoring. With estimated probabilities, asymptotic validity follows from consistent weight or outcome-quantile estimation under the respective regularity conditions. We then quantify retention through the censoring copula, compare joint calibration with coordinatewise bounds and study path selection and estimation. Simulations examine several aspects of the proposed method. Finally, an application to a Canadian joint-life annuity portfolio illustrates one-sided lower prediction bounds for reported first- and second-death times. The five-year observation period puts a limit to the attainable lower bounds, with different limits for different paths; the bounds seem most informative for older annuitants.
item.dc:creator: Martin Bladt

item.title: Vector Copula-Based Markov Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose the Vector Copula-based Markov Model (VCBMM) for describing multivariate time series with nonlinear dependence. To extend univariate copula-based Markov models to multivariate time series, we develop a hierarchical construction based on scalar aggregates and consider the Vector Sklar Theorem to obtain the joint density of the VCBMM. We further assume the Clayton copula for serial dependence and the multivariate Gaussian distribution for the marginals. The corresponding likelihood function and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with the Inference Functions for Margins (IFM) method are provided. The performance of the proposed model is illustrated through simulation studies. In real data analysis, we apply the model to bivariate daily stock returns from the 2008 global financial crisis (2008 GFC) and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic (2020 COVID-19).
item.dc:creator: Li-Hsien Sun, Po-Chun Huang, Po-Cheng Chen, Chi-Yang Chiu

item.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.
item.dc:creator: Max Zhu, Srivathsan Amruth, Sina Akbari, Qingyuan Zhao

item.title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
item.description: arXiv:2610.25405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.
item.dc:creator: Vanessa Rodriguez, Brieuc Lehmann, Karla Diaz-Ordaz

item.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Trials with Irregular and Informative Assessment Times: Marginal Mean Models and Sensitivity Parameter Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.25454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In randomized trials, outcome assessment times often vary across participants and may depend on the underlying outcome process, so outcomes observed near a target time need not represent the target population. Whether assessment is informative cannot be determined from the observed data alone. We extend the sensitivity analysis framework of Smith et al.\ (2024), which is anchored in an explainable assessment assumption and was restricted to continuous outcomes through an identity-link marginal mean model, to a broader class of link functions that accommodates binary and count outcomes. Within this framework, we develop an influence function-based augmented inverse intensity-weighted estimator that is root-$n$ consistent under standard regularity conditions. We also propose a data-driven procedure for selecting the range of the sensitivity parameter from plausible bounds on the target mean outcome and for constructing a confidence set for this range, which accounts for uncertainty in sensitivity parameter selection. We illustrate the method with data from the ARC study and evaluate its finite-sample performance in simulation studies.
item.dc:creator: Yujing Gao, Shu Yang, Ravi Varadhan, Andrew Redd, Andrea J. Apter, Daniel O. Scharfstein

item.title: Multivariate M-extremiles
item.description: arXiv:2610.25492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extremiles represent an important class of distributional functionals defined through weighted squared loss functions, providing a valuable alternative to quantiles and expectiles. To date, their development has remained confined to the univariate setting. Here we introduce a robust multivariate extension of extremiles for random vectors by combining a directional weighting mechanism with Huber's multidimensional loss function. The proposed definition yields a family of directional extremiles indexed by a tuning parameter controlling the degree of robustness to outliers, with the quadratic-loss geometric extremile arising as a limiting case. We prove their main theoretical properties and introduce the notion of extremile sets. From an inferential perspective, we develop an efficient two-step procedure based on iteratively reweighted least squares, and derive asymptotic properties using the theory of Z-estimators. The finite-sample behavior of the proposed methodology is investigated through simulation experiments under Gaussian, contaminated, and heavy-tailed settings. An application to daily returns of three major cryptocurrencies illustrates its practical utility on financial data.
item.dc:creator: Luca Merlo, Valeria Bignozzi, Lea Petrella, Nicola Salvati

item.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2610.25613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend anytime-valid inference for linear models from independent scalar outcomes to units that contribute a vector of dependent outcomes. We develop a parametric and a nonparametric treatment. For the Gaussian multivariate linear model with an unstructured error covariance, we derive a closed-form Bayes factor under the right-Haar prior and a matrix-normal mixture alternative and prove that it is an exact e-value at every sample size and a test martingale in the invariant filtration. To our knowledge, this Bayes factor is new in the generality considered here: a d x q coefficient matrix, nuisance regressors and an arbitrary fixed positive-definite prior precision under the right-Haar nuisance prior. It yields sequential Hotelling and MANOVA tests with exact confidence sequences. Under a common within-cluster design, the cluster-robust Wald statistic of a pooled regression is equal to Hotelling's T^2 statistic computed from the per-cluster least-squares summaries, giving an exact Gaussian benchmark with G-1 degrees of freedom. For general clustered population least-squares projections, the corresponding sandwich statistic is an asymptotic e-process, without Gaussian, common-design or linearity assumptions. Each treatment includes growth and first-order expected stopping-time results; under stronger regularity, direct comparisons of expected log evidence identify a fixed mixture precision that maximizes expected log growth through constant order within a specified family, for a specified frequentist alternative. Applied to randomized experiments with several outcomes, the robust procedure gives asymptotically anytime-valid joint tests, confidence ellipsoids and simultaneous confidence sequences for the vector of average treatment effects from ordinary least-squares estimates and cluster-robust standard errors.
item.dc:creator: Michael Lindon

item.title: Estimation and Inference for the Joint Autoregressive Quantile-Expected Shortfall Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.25730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expected shortfall is defined as the truncated mean of a random variable that falls below a specified quantile level and is widely recognized as an important risk measure. Motivated by the empirical observation of clustering patterns in financial risks, we consider a joint autoregressive model for both conditional quantile and expected shortfall. Existing estimation methods for such models typically rely on minimizing a nonlinear and nonconvex joint loss function, which is challenging to solve. We introduce a two-step regression framework to estimate the model parameters with theoretical guarantees. We further develop a Portmanteau test for model diagnostics and prove its asymptotic validity for Type I error control. Our empirical results on stock market data indicate that the proposed models effectively capture the clustering patterns and leverage effects on the conditional expected shortfall.
item.dc:creator: Peiyao Cai, Kean Ming Tan, Xuming He

item.title: Using Bayesian Sequential Logistic Regression to Model the Organ Transplant Selection Process
item.description: arXiv:2610.25744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organ transplantation evaluation is a multi-stage process in which only patients who complete one stage remain eligible for the next, leading to patient attrition and reducing later-stage sample sizes. Covariate associations may differ across decision points, and identifying these stage-specific effects is necessary to target interventions and understand disparities. Conventional approaches that model each transition independently fail to distinguish stage-specific from shared associations and tend to produce imprecise estimates at later stages. We propose a Bayesian sequential logistic regression (BSLR) framework that represents progression as conditional Bernoulli distributions within a joint likelihood that preserves chronological ordering; we further show its equivalence to an adjusted continuation-ratio model. A hierarchical prior decomposes each covariate effect into an overall effect and a transition-specific deviation. This partial-pooling structure shares information across stages and stabilizes estimation where data are sparse, while a masking mechanism accommodates covariates structurally unavailable at particular stages without discarding records or imputing values. In simulations, BSLR achieved lower bias, posterior variance, and mean squared error than independent logistic regression. We demonstrated the utility of our model using a cohort of patients referred for kidney or liver transplant. Posterior estimates indicated that the associations of clinical indicators and social determinants of health with progression differed across care continuum phases. BSLR identified stage-specific heterogeneity in covariate associations, revealing factors whose effects reversed direction across evaluation stages and detecting associations at late-stage transitions that independent models failed to resolve due to insufficient precision.
item.dc:creator: Xukun Zhu, Tyler Schappe, Ursula Rogers, Roland Matsouaka, Jacqueline B. Henson, Norine W. Chan, Goni Katz-Greenberg, Lisa M. McElroy, Samuel I. Berchuck

item.title: Where to weight? Estimating population causal effects with weighted double score matching in complex surveys
item.description: arXiv:2610.25870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Double score matching is an emerging method for causal inference that combines propensity and prognostic scores to achieve dimension reduction and model robustness. However, when the observational data are drawn from a complex survey, the existing literature does not provide sufficient guidance on the proper use of survey weights in matching strategies for population-level causal inference. We develop weighted double score matching (WDSM) that provides a unified framework for incorporating survey weights throughout the score estimation, matching, and outcome analysis under both retrospective (informative) and prospective (non-informative) sampling designs. We establish asymptotic normality of the resultant effect estimates under both known and estimated scores and develop a linearization-based bootstrap procedure for variance estimation that preserves the survey-weighted matching structure. Simulation studies show that WDSM substantially reduces bias relative to unweighted matching when either the propensity score model or the prognostic score models are correctly specified. Under correct specification, WDSM also improves efficiency and confidence interval coverage relative to survey-weighted propensity score matching, with particularly pronounced gains under poor overlap. Applications to early marijuana use and mental health in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health and to sleep duration and glycemic control in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey illustrate the practical value of WDSM for population-level inference. We conclude with a discussion of our findings and provide practical guidance on incorporating survey weights into matching-based analyses of observational data.
item.dc:creator: Yukang Zeng, Guangyu Tong, Jiaqi Tong, Haidong Lu, Bhramar Mukherjee, Fan Li

item.title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance
item.description: arXiv:2610.26011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang--Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.
item.dc:creator: Fabrizio Maturo, Annamaria Porreca

item.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Multivariate Optimal Sample Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal sample allocation in stratified surveys for a single characteristic is well understood, yet multivariate allocation remains challenging. In the absence of a total order on the precision vector, a decision-maker must balance competing objectives through preference weightings whose effects on the resulting allocation are generally unclear. This paper develops an analytical sensitivity analysis for multivariate optimal allocation based on the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. We show that a stepwise weighted Chebyshev minimisation yields a unique efficient allocation and the normal vector to the Pareto frontier, from which marginal rates of substitution between survey objectives and shadow prices for cost and precision constraints follow directly. The method enables interpretable adjustments to weightings or cost limits when specified allocations do not meet survey purposes. Numerical results on an educational survey quantify the impact of budget and quality constraints on estimation precision and demonstrate how the trade-off information guides iterative refinement of preference weightings.
item.dc:creator: Felix Willems, Ralf M\"unnich

item.title: Causal Robustness from Synthetic Environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.26250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study robust prediction when the training data come from a single observational distribution. Causality-oriented methods for robust prediction usually use heterogeneity across observed environments both to learn an invariant prediction function and to determine the perturbations against which it is robust. We show that both can be recovered from one distribution under a structural additive-noise mechanism for the response. Under the structural model considered here, the causal prediction function has constant conditional mean squared error given its prediction. We generate synthetic environments by reweighting the covariate distribution along the prediction and use a Cram\'er--von Mises criterion to measure departures from this invariance. The resulting penalised risk admits a regularised worst-case representation, linking the criterion to robustness against covariate shifts induced by reweighting observations according to their predicted values. Under an additional orthogonality condition, we identify the causal prediction function as the unique risk minimiser subject to this invariance restriction. We establish consistency and an explicit rate, derive a goodness-of-fit test for the invariance restriction, and characterise the population target under misspecification. With multiple observed environments, the construction applies environment by environment and can be combined with Distributional Robustness via Invariant Gradients (DRIG) to control two complementary classes of shifts.
item.dc:creator: Linying Yang, Cyrill Scheidegger, Xinwei Shen, Peter B\"uhlmann

item.title: Covariate-adaptive randomization using historical data and bootstrap-based inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.26254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR) can improve the efficiency of average treatment effect (ATE) estimation by reducing chance imbalances in prognostic baseline covariates. A recently proposed CAR method that balances multiple covariates, including continuous ones, can achieve optimal precision when the conditional mean of the outcome can be expressed as a linear combination of the covariate features used for the CAR procedure. However, this condition may be difficult to satisfy when the relationship between covariates and the outcome is nonlinear. Furthermore, directly balancing multiple covariates may reduce estimation precision in finite samples. We propose three CAR methods that incorporate a prognostic score learned from individual-level historical data into their imbalance measures. The prognostic score reduces multiple covariates to one dimension while giving larger weights to covariates that are more strongly associated with the outcome. Another challenge with CAR is difficulty in inference due to dependence between subjects induced by the CAR procedure. Existing bootstrap-based inference methods emulate the CAR design by reassigning treatment within each bootstrap sample, which causes difficulty in interval estimation under CAR with continuous covariates. We propose a bootstrap method with unequal probability resampling corresponding to the CAR design, avoiding reassignment within each bootstrap sample. In simulations, the proposed CAR methods reduced prognostic imbalance, thereby improving estimation precision compared to existing assignment designs, and the proposed bootstrap method accurately assessed estimation uncertainty under our proposed CAR. An application to Clazosentan trials demonstrated that the proposed CAR methods similarly improved prognostic balance, and the proposed bootstrap method closely reproduced the distribution induced by the proposed CAR.
item.dc:creator: Nodoka Seya, Masataka Taguri, Osamu Togo, Kengo Kamatani

item.title: Incorporating therapist capacity, availability and turnover in trials of therapist-delivered interventions: Non-orthogonal factorial designs
item.description: arXiv:2610.26321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disentangling therapist from intervention effects has long been considered a challenge in randomised trials of therapist delivered interventions. When separating these effects is of interest, factorial designs have been proposed in which therapists and interventions are regarded as two potentially interacting components of a complex intervention, represented by two treatment factors (one random, one fixed). In these trial designs, every therapist delivers each intervention, and patients are randomised to the resulting therapist intervention combinations. It is assumed that each therapist is allocated the same number of patients (equal capacity), that all therapists in a centre are available when a patient is randomised (equal availability), and that therapists remain involved for the entire duration of the trial (no turnover). In practice, these are strong assumptions that may lead to delayed or suspended randomisation and increased trial costs. We propose three novel randomisation strategies that explicitly account for therapist capacity, availability, and turnover while maintaining desirable statistical properties. In a simulation study, we compared the proposed and existing randomisation strategies across trial scenarios and design parameters, assessing trade offs between operational efficiency and statistical performance. The results provide practical guidance for trialists designing trials of therapist delivered interventions under real world constraints.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Singh, Rebecca EA Walwyn, Steven G Gilmour

item.title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests
item.description: arXiv:2610.26728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.
item.dc:creator: Javier Enrique Aguilar, Daniel Klippert, Yusufhan Balci, Alexander Marx

item.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking
item.description: arXiv:2610.26796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
item.dc:creator: Yujia Liu, Yuanyuan Lin, Ruijian Han, Yiming Xu

item.title: Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control for Stable Counterfactual Estimation under Donor Redundancy
item.description: arXiv:2610.24113v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthetic control methods estimate counterfactual outcomes by weighting untreated donor units to match a treated unit before treatment. In recent applications, however, the donor pool can be large, highly correlated, and short in pre-treatment history, yielding many near-equivalent solutions with unstable and difficult-to-interpret donor weights. We propose Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control (Graph-SC), a convex estimator that augments the classical pre-treatment matching objective with a graph Laplacian penalty. The graph encodes similarity among donor trajectories, encouraging coherent weights over structurally related donors while preserving the transparency of synthetic controls. We provide theoretical results characterizing the bias-variance tradeoff induced by graph regularization and establish efficient convergence guarantees with an accelerated proximal gradient method. Across a controlled simulation under donor redundancy, the California Proposition 99 benchmark, and observational counterfactual analyses on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, Graph-SC improves weight stability, reduces sensitivity to redundant donor pools, and maintains competitive pre- and post-treatment accuracy relative to classical and regularized synthetic control baselines. Our results suggest that graph regularization is most valuable not as a universal accuracy booster, but as a principled mechanism for selecting stable and interpretable counterfactuals from near-equivalent synthetic controls with comparable pre-treatment fit.
item.dc:creator: Yanlin Zhang, Sungyong Chung, Alireza Talebpour

item.title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.24233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.
item.dc:creator: Jianbin Tan, Xingran Chen, Kevin He, Zhenke Wu, Bhramar Mukherjee, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: Computational Taxonomy for visualizing and exploring systems with functional response dynamics: soybean's O2-respiration example
item.description: arXiv:2610.24310v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A collective of 1684 O2-respiration curves of 183 dimensions are collected along soybeans' germinating process with 72 covariate feature-measurements. We develop a computational thematic platform for first discovering and exposing heterogeneous typical-shapes and then extracting readable, visible and explainable pattern information with biological implications when comparing between them. Via existing knowledge on seeds of much smaller sizes, such collective of O2-respiration curves are expected to generally embrace the two-stage or sigmoidal patterns. However, due to Soybean's relatively large surface area with harder to control and retain experimental conditions, much diverse and heterogeneous shapes are highly expected. Shannon entropy is applied to capture potential categorical nature across the 183 time-points, while scaled mutual information is used to evaluate pattern-consistency. Three motifs are determined to partition the temporal time-points into three regions: W1 on [1, 20], W2 on [21, 60] and W3 on [61, 183]. Each curve is partitioned into three segments accordingly. Hierarchical cluster algorithm is applied onto these motif-region-specific curve-segments, respectively. Five clusters of shapes on W1 are selected, four on W2 and four on W3. We computationally build a tree-geometry-based Taxonomic Hierarchy to organize these 80 curve-shapes into 15 typical shapes. Then we compare among these typical shapes to extract and display their differences through block-sustained heatmaps. Each focal block is expressed va a network of covariate features to reveal dominant interacting effects of various orders. Scientific explanations and understanding are to be rested on the collected heatmaps and coupled networks collectively.
item.dc:creator: Eric Goldman, Thomas B. Michelon, Fushing Hsieh

item.title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses
item.description: arXiv:2610.24463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A rare 3D human pose in a motion sequence may reflect either a genuine movement or an estimation error, making correction difficult when reference databases contain few comparable examples. We investigate whether local geometric structure can support the recovery and generation of rare configura- tions, using motion-capture sequences from AMASS, which unifies datasets through a common parametric human-body model, together with video-based pose estimates. We develop the cylindrical manifold attention transformer (CMAT), which extends local manifold fitting through geometry- and task- dependent neighborhood weights. For motion correction, Self-Action CMAT draws on comparable windows within a sequence, adjusts their contributions for neighborhood imbalance and temporal dependence, and integrates local geometry with robust temporal regularization. Experiments on perturbed and estimated motions show reductions in position and acceleration errors, with component analyses examining how weighting and temporal processing con- tribute to recovery. The controlled correction comparisons are exploratory and conditional on the selected motion-amplitude bound. For generation, Rarity-preserving CMAT explores locally supported configurations subject to independently calibrated rarity and separation from stored observations. Under common screening criteria, it achieves a higher yield of eligible rare poses than the evaluated generation baselines.
item.dc:creator: Feiyue Pan, Zhigang Yao

item.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
item.description: arXiv:2610.24586v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.
item.dc:creator: Agus Sudjianto, Denis Burakov

item.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.24787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Rooijakkers, Edwin Fong

item.title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.25421v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, existing rank- and graph-based estimators can suffer from substantial bias under general dependence, limiting their usefulness for statistical inference. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Holger Dette, Fang Han

item.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
item.description: arXiv:2610.25667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two for their compliers. We discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.
item.dc:creator: Tetsuya Kaji

item.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization
item.description: arXiv:2610.25821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Orabona

item.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.25997v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.
item.dc:creator: Wanjie Wang

item.title: Depth based on translates of a convex body: geometry, floating bodies, and empirical theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.26108v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a fixed full-dimensional convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, we study the $K$-depth of a point $y$ with respect to a probability measure $\mu$ by comparing the masses of translates of $K$ that fail to contain $y$. Its upper level sets are intersections of high-mass translates of $K$, and hence are convex and admit an exact representation as Minkowski erosions. We distinguish the closed core determined by the maximisers of the translation-mass function from the effective support on which the depth exceeds its unavoidable baseline. We establish continuity, affine equivariance, comparison with halfspace (Tukey) depth, and normal-cone and smoothness criteria. For uniform measures on convex bodies, the regions coincide exactly with the ball floating bodies of Sch\"utt, Werner and Yalikun; for positive continuous densities they coincide with the weighted ball floating bodies of Werner and Yalikun. For dilates $tK$, the depth converges to a depth generated by the tangent cones of $K$ as $t \to \infty$; for smooth $K$ this limit is Tukey's halfspace depth, whereas nonsmooth testing bodies can produce a genuinely different limit. The worst-case maximal $K$-depth is exactly $1/h_T(K)$, where $h_T(K)$ is the Helly number of the family of translates of $K$. Under a uniform interior rolling-ball condition and compact support and having zero mass on hyperplanes, the convergence to halfspace depth is monotone and uniform with an explicit error bound. If the density is bounded by $L$, then this bound is of order $O(t^{-1})$ and this order is sharp. We also record that the dependence on the testing body is not monotone in general, while Hausdorff perturbations of $K$ give stable depth functions and regions at regular levels. Finally, we prove uniform consistency and pointwise weak limits for empirical $K$-depth, including the non-Gaussian limit caused by nonunique active translates.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Molchanov, Stanislav Nagy

item.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.26361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.
item.dc:creator: Zekai Li, Mauricio Barahona, Philipp Thomas

item.title: R2-GP: Variance-Calibrated Priors for Additive Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.26437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop R2-GP, an R2D2-type prior for Gaussian process (GP) generalised additive models (GAMs) that calibrates explained variance ($R^2$) for Mat\'ern covariance kernels. The function variance for standard Mat\'ern kernels depends jointly on the effect magnitude and length-scale. As such, smooth and rough components with identical amplitudes contribute very different amounts of variation. With independent priors on component amplitudes, this variation results in variance overestimation, especially in higher dimensions. We overcome this by taking direct control over each component's expected contribution to prior explained variance. We do this by rescaling each component based on its length scale and observed inputs, and modelling each rescaled variance as a share of the function variance induced by a global $R^2$ prior. This allows R2-GP to scale well to many components. To also scale to large sample sizes, we extend R2-GP to Hilbert space approximation methods, a framework for kernels exploiting their spectral decompositions for fast and efficient inference. Our simulations and real-world case studies demonstrate superior generalisation and parameter recovery over independent variance priors.
item.dc:creator: Javier Enrique Aguilar, Soham Mukherjee, David Kohns

item.title: Synthetic Control: An Exact Geometric Formulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26576v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The synthetic control method matches a treated unit to a convex combination of donor units, with the relative importance of each predictor determined by a weight matrix $V$. In standard practice, $V$ is selected through a bi-level optimization problem that is nonconvex and lacks convergence guarantees. This article derives an exact geometric solution for synthetic control estimators. For any positive definite $V$, a synthetic control is given by the projection of the treated unit's predictors onto the convex hull of the donor predictors under a $V$-weighted norm. As $V$ varies over its candidate class, these projections trace out the set of attainable synthetic controls. We characterize this set. When the predictor vector of the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of the donor predictors, the attainable set under general positive definite $V$ is the union of the facets of the donor hull that are visible from the treated unit. For diagonal $V$, a sign-compatibility test identifies the attainable set. When the treated unit lies inside the hull, exact matches exist. We select the one that minimizes the average of the pairwise matching discrepancies between the treated unit and each of the donors contributing to the synthetic control. These characterizations replace bi-level optimization with a fast enumeration method that is guaranteed to deliver the global optimum over the attainable set. Moreover, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions for the selection of donor weights characterize the set of positive definite predictor weight matrices that rationalize any given set of donor weights. Applications to the California tobacco control program and to the economic effects of German reunification illustrate the advantages of the proposed procedure over existing practice.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Abadie, Yucheng Shang

item.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2402.11936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nested sampling is widely used in astrophysics and cosmology to reliably infer model parameters and compare models within a Bayesian framework. To address models with many parameters, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) random walks are used within nested sampling to advance a live point population. Diagnostics for nested sampling inference are essential to verify that trustworthy astrophysical conclusions can be drawn. We develop a diagnostic to identify poorly mixed random walks that do not meet the requirements of nested sampling. The distance from the start to the end of the random walk, the jump distance, is compared to the typical neighbour distance between live points, to obtain a relative jump distance (RJD). A robust estimate of a typical neighbour Mahalanobis distance is obtained with the MLFriends algorithm. In mock and real-world inference applications such as inferring the distance to GW170817, we observe the relative jump distance. We propose the geometric mean <RJD> and fraction of RJD>1 as new summary diagnostics. To evaluate the sensitivity of the new diagnostics, problematic runs are identified by comparison with reruns using much longer MCMC chains. Trustworthy inference runs are consistently associated with <RJD> above 1.1, while problematic runs can fall below these thresholds. The RJD is more sensitive than previous tests based on the live point insertion order. The RJD diagnostic is proposed as a widely applicable diagnostic to verify inference with nested sampling. It is implemented in the UltraNest package in version 4.1.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Buchner

item.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference
item.description: arXiv:2405.07979v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Variance reduction for causal inference in the presence of network interference is often achieved through either outcome modeling, typically analyzed under unit-randomized Bernoulli designs, or clustered experimental designs, typically analyzed without strong parametric assumptions. In this work, we study the intersection of these two approaches and make the following threefold contributions. First, we present an estimator of the total treatment effect (or global average treatment effect) in low-order outcome models when the data are collected under general experimental designs, generalizing previous results for Bernoulli designs. We refer to this estimator as the pseudoinverse estimator and give bounds on its bias and variance in terms of properties of the experimental design. Second, we evaluate these bounds for the case of Bernoulli graph cluster randomized (GCR) designs. Its variance scales like the smaller of the variance obtained by the estimator derived under a low-order assumption, and the variance obtained from cluster randomization, showing that combining these variance reduction strategies is preferable to using either individually. When the order of the potential outcomes model is correctly specified, our estimator is always unbiased, and under a misspecified model, we upper bound the bias by the closeness of the ground truth model to a low-order model. Third, we give empirical evidence that our variance bounds can be used to select a good clustering that minimizes the worst-case variance under a cluster randomized design from a set of candidate clusterings. Across a range of graphs and clustering algorithms, our method consistently selects clusterings that perform well on a range of response models, suggesting the practical use of our bounds.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Eichhorn, Samir Khan, Johan Ugander, Christina Lee Yu

item.title: Data Sketching and Stacking: A Confluence of Two Strategies for Predictive Inference in Gaussian Process Regressions with High-Dimensional Features
item.description: arXiv:2406.18681v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article focuses on drawing computationally-efficient predictive inference from Gaussian process (GP) regressions with a large number of features when the response is conditionally independent of the features given the projection to a noisy low dimensional manifold. Bayesian estimation of the regression relationship using Markov Chain Monte Carlo and subsequent predictive inference is computationally prohibitive and may lead to inferential inaccuracies since accurate variable selection is essentially impossible in such high-dimensional GP regressions.
